A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same incremental causal-effect framework and methotrexate application. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original Monte Carlo results in Section 4.1, an analysis of 1010 rheumatoid arthritis patients in Section 4.2, and model diagnostics in Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 reports revised Monte Carlo results, retains the original clinical analysis and diagnostics, and adds simulation results in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The hazard-multiplication intervention, causal estimand, plug-in IPW estimator and bootstrap inference procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C evaluates covariate-dependent interventions already permitted by v1's general definition of θ(t,L).

E1.justification: Appendix C adds a synthetic scenario with uniform, normal and Bernoulli covariates and covariate-dependent interventions, extending evaluation beyond constant hazard multipliers. The original simulation task and the same 1010-patient clinical population remain.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically benchmarks the proposed estimator against competing estimators. V2's discussion of IPW least squares and proximal recursive least squares describes prior work, not additional evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The simulation protocols are substantively revised and expanded. Section 4.1 replaces T_i with min(T_i,2) in the stated outcome-generating mean and adds percent bias as a metric. Appendix C introduces a three-covariate generating model and nine heterogeneous intervention specifications. The PDFs do not establish whether the original formula revision reflects changed implementation or corrected documentation.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a sensitivity analysis of estimator accuracy and interval coverage across nine coefficient vectors for covariate-dependent interventions with mixed covariates. The existing sample-size analysis and Appendix B's Schoenfeld, Cox-Aalen and martingale diagnostics are retained.

E5.justification: The original simulation retains 1000 Monte Carlo datasets and 200 multiplier-bootstrap replicates. The additional simulation specifies 5000 datasets and 50 bootstrap replicates, using the existing standard-error and Wald-interval coverage reporting approach. This is a new experiment's replication design, not an increase in runs for the original experiment.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially replaces bias, standard-error and coverage entries, changes bias/SE scale annotations from 10^-3 to 10^-2, and adds target values and percent biases. For example, coverage at n=200 and θ=1/3 changes from 95.0% to 93.0%. Table 3 adds heterogeneous-intervention results. These are revised or added results, not established same-setting performance changes; clinical estimates and diagnostics remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 corrects the integration-by-parts expression from θ to θ−1 in the boundary terms and uses |θ−1| in the subsequent bound. The regularity conditions now printed in Theorems 2–3 already appeared in v1's proofs; their relocation introduces no new assumptions or theorems.

C1.justification: Both versions claim identification of continuous-time incremental effects without positivity under consistency and no unmeasured confounding, together with IPW estimation and root-n inference. The principal contribution and clinical conclusions remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 expands the explanation of why interventions on treatment distributions avoid positivity requirements. Section 4.2 interprets the unchanged methotrexate findings through Tchetgen Tchetgen et al.'s tender-joint analysis instead of Choi et al.'s study. Appendix C also extends the favorable inference interpretation, although its reported coverage remains near 94% rather than the nominal 95%.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly states that the simulation estimates cumulative hazards using a Cox proportional hazards model; v1 explicitly documented Cox fitting only for the clinical application. Appendix C supplies its generating distributions, coefficients and intervention vectors. Clinical data-processing instructions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works remain the same after matching citation suffix changes. V2 explicitly distinguishes Nie et al.'s discrete-time setting and replaces the clinical interpretation's reference to Choi et al. with a more detailed comparison to Tchetgen Tchetgen et al. These are limited positioning refinements.

P1.justification: The introduction is reorganized around the existing probationer example, removing the technology-review motivation and clarifying positivity and observed treatment distributions. Regularity conditions move into the theorem statements, with additional notation explanations and copyediting. Most substantive exposition and the conclusion remain intact.

P2.justification: The whole paper adopts ICLR formatting, changing typography, author layout, headers and display sizing and placement. Table 1 gains rows, Table 3 is added, and Appendix B consolidates previously separated displays. All five figure images are unchanged. The new Table 3 labels θ as β′l although its accompanying text specifies exp(β′l).

improvement.justification: V2 modestly improves empirical support and precision through the heterogeneous-intervention simulation, the Appendix A.2 algebra correction, and clearer simulation documentation. The method and clinical findings remain stable. The gains are limited by Table 3's inconsistent intervention label and its claim of nominal coverage despite values near 94%; these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the useful additions and corrections.
